fields.title: Understanding Economics
fields.body:
Economics explains how societies decide what to produce, how to produce it and who gets it.

It starts with scarcity: resources are limited, so every choice has a cost.

Understanding these basics helps you read the news, manage money and make better decisions at work.
fields.summary: A short introduction to how economies work.

fields.title: Exploring Global Markets
fields.body:
Global markets let countries specialise in what they produce best and trade for the rest.

Exchange rates link prices across borders. A weaker currency makes exports cheaper and imports more expensive.

Supply chains spread production across many countries, which lowers costs but adds risk.
fields.summary: How trade connects countries and prices.

fields.title: Market Trends
fields.body:
Market trends are long movements in prices, demand or behaviour.

Watch interest rates, inflation and employment data: they move many markets at once.

Short-term noise is common, so look at several months of data before calling a trend.
fields.summary: Signals to watch in today's markets.

fields.title: How to Analyze Market Trends
fields.body:
Start with a clear question, then pick data that answers it.

Plot the data over time and compare it with a benchmark, like the market average.

Check for seasonality and one-off events before drawing conclusions.
fields.summary: A simple method to read market data.

fields.title: What is economics?
fields.content:
Economics studies how people, companies and governments use limited resources to meet unlimited wants.

Every choice has an opportunity cost: the value of the best option you give up. Choosing to study tonight costs you the time you could spend working or resting.

Microeconomics looks at individual households and firms. Macroeconomics looks at the whole economy: growth, inflation and unemployment.

fields.title: Supply and demand
fields.content:
Demand shows how much buyers want at each price. When the price rises, people usually buy less.

Supply shows how much sellers offer at each price. Higher prices encourage firms to produce more.

The market price settles where supply equals demand. A shortage pushes prices up; a surplus pushes prices down.

fields.title: Thinking like an economist
fields.content:
Economists ask what incentives people face. A small change in cost or reward can change behaviour a lot.

Think at the margin: compare the extra benefit of one more unit with its extra cost, not the total.

Sunk costs are money or time already spent that cannot be recovered. Good decisions ignore them.

fields.title: Checking claims and data
fields.content:
Correlation is not causation. Ice cream sales and drowning both rise in summer, but one does not cause the other.

Always ask about the sample: who was measured, how many, and when.

Look for the counterfactual: what would have happened without the policy or event?

fields.title: Building a budget
fields.content:
A budget lists your income and planned spending for a month. Start with fixed costs like rent, then variable costs like food.

The 50/30/20 rule is a simple guide: 50% needs, 30% wants, 20% savings and debt repayment.

Track spending for a few weeks before setting limits, so your budget matches real habits.

fields.title: Saving and interest
fields.content:
Interest is the price of money over time. Savers earn interest; borrowers pay it.

Compound interest means you earn interest on past interest, so money grows faster the longer you save.

Inflation reduces what money can buy. A savings rate below inflation means your real savings shrink.

fields.title: Key economic vocabulary
fields.content:
GDP (gross domestic product) is the total value of goods and services produced in a country in a year.

Inflation is a general rise in prices. Deflation is a general fall in prices.

Unemployment rate is the share of people who want a job and are actively looking but do not have one.

fields.title: Explaining numbers clearly
fields.content:
Round numbers and compare them to something familiar: "about the price of a coffee a day".

Say whether a change is in percent or percentage points. Interest rising from 2% to 3% is one percentage point, but a 50% increase.

Use one chart for one message, and label the axes.

fields.title: Communicating value
fields.content:
Customers buy outcomes, not features. Explain what problem your product solves and for whom.

Price signals quality. Discounts can raise sales now but may lower the value customers expect later.

Trust lowers transaction costs: clear terms and honest claims make people decide faster.

fields.title: Negotiation basics
fields.content:
Know your BATNA, the best alternative to a negotiated agreement. It sets the point where you walk away.

Look for trades: give what is cheap for you but valuable to the other side.

Anchoring matters: the first number mentioned often shapes the final deal.

fields.title: What is money?
fields.content:
Money has three functions: a medium of exchange, a unit of account and a store of value.

Modern money is mostly digital bank deposits, created when banks make loans.

Central banks manage the money supply and set policy interest rates to keep inflation stable.

fields.title: Inflation and your wallet
fields.content:
When inflation is high, the same salary buys fewer goods. This is a fall in real income.

Central banks raise interest rates to cool demand and slow inflation; borrowing becomes more expensive.

Diversifying savings across assets helps protect purchasing power over the long term.
